_note: Junior Astronaut Academy: 8 short lessons a cadet takes before commanding the outpost. Every fact cites a {title,url} and names the repo data file(s) it comes from (`from`, relative to backend/data); tests check that every number in a fact appears in those files (or is recomputed, for `calc`). Steps accept voice or taps; see app/academy/grade.py for the accept types.
title: Junior Astronaut Academy

lessons.title: Know your Moon
lessons.brief: The next crews will land near the south pole, by a crater called Shackleton.

facts.text: NASA's 2024 list of 9 possible landing regions near the south pole includes Malapert Massif and de Gerlache Rim 2.

source.title: NASA Provides Update on Artemis III Moon Landing Regions (Oct 2024)

facts.text: The far side is the half of the Moon that never faces Earth.

source.title: IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature

facts.text: Shackleton is a crater about 21 km wide and about 4 km deep, right at the Moon's south pole.

source.title: IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature: Shackleton

facts.text: Its floor never gets sunlight, so it is colder than -170 C and can hold ice.

source.title: NASA: Ice confirmed at the Moon's poles (M3 / Chandrayaan-1, 2018)

steps.prompt: The near side always faces Earth. Now find the south pole.
steps.hint: The south pole is at the very bottom.
steps.success: Roger. The south pole. The Sun barely rises there.

steps.prompt: Now tap Shackleton crater, inside the gold ring.
steps.hint: Spin the Moon and find the gold ring.
steps.success: Copy. Shackleton, 21 km wide.

steps.prompt: Why do crews want to land near Shackleton?

options.label: Its dark floor may hold ice

steps.hint: What stays frozen where sunlight never reaches?
steps.success: Correct. Ice can become water and air.

steps.prompt: Space word: mare. What does it mean?
steps.hint: The dark patches you see from Earth.
steps.success: Yes. A mare is a dark plain of old lava.

lessons.title: Talk on the radio
lessons.brief: Radio is noisy, so crews keep it short. Copy means I heard you.

facts.text: Artemis II and Houston really say it: "Houston, we have you loud and clear." ... "Houston copies all."

source.title: NASA Artemis II audio: Houston, We Have You Loud and Clear

steps.prompt: What does "copy" mean on the radio?
steps.hint: It's about hearing.
steps.success: Roger. Copy means I heard you.

steps.prompt: CAPCOM: "Commander, set the shields to 40 percent." Read it back.
steps.capcom: Commander, set the shields to 40 percent.
steps.hint: Repeat what, and how much.
steps.success: Good readback. Shields to 40.

steps.prompt: CAPCOM: "Send the rover for ice." Start your readback with roger.
steps.hint: Roger first, then the order.
steps.success: Perfect readback.

steps.prompt: Static! You missed the last order. What do you say?
steps.hint: Two words. The second one is again.
steps.success: Copy. Say again asks for a repeat.

lessons.title: Power from the Sun
lessons.brief: The outpost runs on solar panels and batteries. No Sun means batteries only.

facts.text: Shackleton Crater Rim gets sunlight about 86% of the time; Malapert Massif about 73%.

source.title: Bussey et al. 2010, Illumination conditions of the south pole of the Moon derived using Kaguya topography, Icarus 208

facts.text: In our 10-day mission window in April 2026, Malapert was in sunlight only 35% of the time.

source.title: JPL Horizons API

facts.text: Its longest night in that window lasted 157 hours, more than 6 days.

source.title: JPL Horizons API

steps.prompt: Which site gets more sunlight?
steps.hint: Bigger number, more sunshine.
steps.success: Correct. More sun, more power.

steps.prompt: Malapert's longest night lasted 157 hours. What keeps the lights on?
steps.hint: What stores power for later?
steps.success: Right. Batteries carry you through the night.
steps.fail: Not that one. Panels need the Sun.

steps.prompt: Night is coming. Move power to the heaters so the pipes don't freeze.
steps.hint: Ask for more power to the heaters.
steps.success: Copy. Heaters up. Pipes stay warm.
steps.fail: Negative. The heaters need more power.

steps.prompt: Space word. Listen: the line between the Moon's day and night. Which word?
steps.hint: Solar panels near it see a low Sun.
steps.success: Yes. The terminator, where day meets night.
steps.fail: Listen again: day side, night side.

lessons.title: Radiation and storms
lessons.brief: We measure radiation dose in mSv. One mSv is about 10 chest x-rays.

facts.text: On the Moon's surface, the Chang'e 4 lander measured 1369 microsieverts a day, about 2.6 times more than inside the ISS.

source.title: Zhang et al. 2020, First measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface, Science Advances 6:eaaz1334

facts.text: On 2024-05-10 a huge solar storm gave Earth bright auroras. It also threw out fast particles and a CME at 1561 km/s.

source.title: DONKI 2024-05-10T15:00:00-GST-001 (NASA CCMC)

facts.text: Regolith, the Moon's dusty soil, stops storm particles well. Scientists have studied covering a base with it.

source.title: NASA NTRS 19890004839, Solar-flare shielding with regolith at a lunar-base site

steps.prompt: What is an mSv?
steps.hint: Think of x-rays.
steps.success: Correct. One mSv is about 10 chest x-rays.

steps.prompt: A big solar storm is coming. What protects the crew best?
steps.hint: Moon soil stops the particles.
steps.success: Right. Soil makes a great shield.
steps.fail: Too risky. What stops the particles?

steps.prompt: Alert! A solar particle storm, like the real one in May 2024. Your order?
steps.hint: Get the whole crew under cover.
steps.success: Copy. Crew in the shelter. Dose rate way down.
steps.fail: Say again? The crew needs the shelter.

lessons.title: Air, water and ice
lessons.brief: Life support makes air and water. Water is heavy to ship. Moon ice could help.

facts.text: In 2009 NASA crashed a 2000 kg Centaur rocket into Cabeus crater near the south pole. It threw up roughly 350 metric tons of material.

source.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: LCROSS

facts.text: The LCROSS spacecraft flew through the dust cloud, and its measurements showed water near the south pole.

source.title: NASA Science: LCROSS

steps.prompt: Where did LCROSS find water?

options.label: Cabeus crater, near the south pole

steps.hint: A dark crater near the south pole.
steps.success: Correct. Dark, cold craters keep ice.
steps.fail: Not that one. Think dark and cold.

steps.prompt: Tap where the LCROSS rocket crashed, near the south pole.
steps.hint: Look just above the pole for the marker.
steps.success: Roger. Cabeus, where water was found.

steps.prompt: Life support is getting low. Send the rover for ice!
steps.hint: The rover can dig up ice.
steps.success: Copy. Rover rolling out for ice.
steps.fail: Negative. The rover needs to fetch ice.

lessons.title: Lessons from Apollo
lessons.brief: Every mission teaches the next. Apollo 12 landed beside an old robot, Surveyor 3.

facts.text: Surveyor 3 sent 6,326 pictures. In 1969 Apollo 12 astronauts walked over and took about 10 kg of parts home, including its TV camera.

source.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Surveyor 3

facts.text: Jim Lovell commanded Apollo 13 and flew around the Moon on Apollo 8.

source.title: NASA Artemis II audio: Message from Apollo Astronaut Jim Lovell

facts.text: John Young and Charlie Duke drove the Apollo 16 rover 26.7 km across the Moon's highlands.

source.title: NSSDCA: Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle

facts.text: Artemis II flew its crew around the Moon in April 2026; the crew audio in this app is theirs.

source.title: NASA Artemis Audio Library

steps.prompt: What did the Apollo 12 crew take home from Surveyor 3?
steps.hint: Surveyor 3 took 6,326 pictures. With what?
steps.success: Correct. Scientists studied what the Moon did to it.
steps.fail: Not that one. It took pictures.

steps.prompt: Listen to Jim Lovell. Which mission first took him around the Moon?
steps.hint: Listen for the mission name.
steps.success: Roger. Apollo 8 was the first crew around the Moon.

steps.prompt: Listen to Charlie Duke. Who landed on the Moon with him?
steps.hint: He names his partner right away.
steps.success: Correct. John Young and Charlie Duke drove their rover 26.7 km.

steps.prompt: Fill the blank: "Astronaut boot prints stay in the Moon's dusty soil, the ____."

accept.sentence: Astronaut boot prints stay in the Moon's dusty soil, the ____.

steps.hint: It starts with r.
steps.success: Right. Regolith, the Moon's dusty soil.

lessons.title: Space words
lessons.brief: The Artemis II crew really used these words. Learn them and talk like the crew.

facts.text: The Artemis II crew said "albedo" while describing the Aristarchus Plateau.

source.title: NASA Artemis II crew audio: Aristarchus Plateau: Color and Limb Relief Observations

facts.text: The crew talked about "regolith" while studying the rays around Ohm Crater.

source.title: NASA Artemis II crew audio: Ohm Crater: Ray Systems and Texture Analysis

facts.text: The crew saw Earth rise from behind the Moon and cheered.

source.title: NASA Artemis II crew audio: Crew Reacts Joyfully to Earth Rise from Behind the Moon

steps.prompt: Listen: a round hole made when a space rock crashed in. Which word?
steps.hint: Tycho is one.
steps.success: Yes. A crater.

steps.prompt: What does albedo mean?
steps.hint: It's about light.
steps.success: Right. Albedo is how bright or dark a surface is.

steps.prompt: Say this word back to me: regolith.
steps.hint: Three parts: reg, oh, lith.
steps.success: Great. Regolith is the Moon's dusty, rocky soil.

steps.prompt: Fill the blank: "When Earth comes up over the Moon's edge, the crew sees an ____."

accept.sentence: When Earth comes up over the Moon's edge, the crew sees an ____.

steps.hint: Like a sunrise, but it's Earth.
steps.success: Yes. Earthrise.
steps.fail: Is Earth coming up, or going down?

steps.prompt: What does terminator mean on the Moon?
steps.hint: A line between light and dark.
steps.success: Correct. The terminator splits day from night.

lessons.title: Check ride
lessons.brief: Your check ride: two days at Shackleton Rim. A real solar storm is coming.

facts.text: The storm in this ride is based on the real storm of 2024-05-10, which gave Earth huge auroras.

source.title: DONKI 2024-05-10T15:00:00-GST-001 (NASA CCMC)

steps.prompt: Day 1. Houston sees an active region on the Sun. Power up the shields.
steps.hint: Ask for more power to the shields.
steps.success: Copy. Shields up.
steps.fail: Negative. The shields need more power.

steps.prompt: Solar particle storm! Based on the real May 2024 storm. Your order?
steps.hint: Get the whole crew under cover.
steps.success: Copy. Crew in the shelter.

steps.prompt: The storm has passed. Bring the crew out of the shelter.
steps.hint: The crew can leave the shelter now.
steps.success: Copy. Crew is out. Back to work.

steps.prompt: Life support is dropping. Send the rover for ice before day 2 ends.
steps.hint: The rover can dig up ice.
steps.success: Copy. Rover rolling out for ice.
steps.fail: Negative. The rover needs to fetch ice.
